item.title: Desire to Move Permanently to U.S. at New Low (107 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/708614/desire-migrate-drops-new-low.aspx, See on Hacker News

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. remains the most desired destination for people who would like to leave their own countries permanently, but Gallup's latest data show it is less attractive than it once was.

In 2025, 15% of adults worldwide who say they would like to move permanently to another country name the U.S. as their preferred destination, the lowest level recorded in nearly two decades of Gallup research. From 2007 to 2009, 24% of would-be migrants named the U.S. as their top choice, and that figure remained near 20% through 2016. Since 2017, it has been at or below 18%.

The rank order of the countries attracting the most interest from potential migrants has seen little change since Gallup’s first measure. Canada ranks second, as it has for several years, with 9% of potential migrants mentioning the U.S. neighbor. The appeal of these desired destinations did not change in 2025, even as the U.S. became less desirable.

Line charts show trends in the percentage of adults worldwide who would like to move permanently to top destination countries from 2007–2009 to 2025. The United States remains the top destination but declines from 24% to 15%. Canada rises from 7% to 9%. The United Kingdom declines from 7% to 4%. Germany, Australia, Spain, France, Japan, Italy, and Saudi Arabia remain broadly stable around 3% to 5%.

Gallup's latest update on migration desire is based on a question asked almost annually: “Ideally, if you had the opportunity, would you like to move permanently to another country, or would you prefer to continue living in this country?” Those who say they would like to move are then asked to name their preferred destination.

Results for 2025 are based on interviews with over 144,000 adults in 140 countries. The current estimates include data from China for 2023, the last time the question was asked there.

The most recent analysis period coincides with a sharp slowdown in international migration into the U.S., amid changes in immigration policy and declining migration desire in several regions. External data suggest global migration more broadly slowed in 2024 after surging post-pandemic.

Declining Desire to Move to the U.S.

The U.S. became less attractive to adults in several regions in 2025, with statistically significant declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia.

Latin America accounts for seven of the 16 countries worldwide where the percentage naming the U.S. as a preferred destination fell by at least 10 points. In the region, the percentage fell from 33% in 2024 to 28% in 2025.

Other Latin American countries that saw double-digit declines include U.S. neighbor Mexico, where the latest 21% who want to move to the U.S. matches the previous low set in 2017 and 2018. In Honduras, desire to migrate to the U.S. dropped 35 percentage points, from 71% to 36%, the largest decline in any country in 2025.

###Embeddable###

Despite the falling numbers, the U.S. remains by far the most desired destination in Latin America and the Caribbean and in sub-Saharan Africa. The picture varies more in other regions.

In Southeast Asia, Japan leads at 23%, compared with 12% for the U.S. In the Middle East and North Africa, Germany attracts 13% and Saudi Arabia 12% of potential migrants, with the U.S. at 9%. In South Asia, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. are roughly tied, each cited by 7%. Within the European Union, Spain, at 11%, and Switzerland, at 8%, rank ahead of the U.S., at 6%.

Global Desire to Migrate Falls, Shifts

Beyond where people want to go, the data also show a shift in how many want to move at all.

Overall, global desire to migrate declined in 2025 to its lowest level in a decade, driven by sharp drops in regions that have long had the highest migration aspirations, including Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. After holding at a record-high 16% between 2021 and 2024, global desire dipped in 2025 for the first time in years, falling one point to 15%, a level not seen since 2018.

###Embeddable###

In Latin America and the Caribbean, 25% of adults say they would like to move permanently to another country, the lowest level in a decade. The decline is particularly notable in this region, where migration desire has fallen steadily after peaking at 34% in 2021-2022.

Multiple countries across the region recorded double-digit declines between 2024 and 2025. In Honduras and El Salvador, the percentage of adults wanting to leave fell sharply last year, from levels above 50% in several prior years to 35% and 25%, respectively.

In sub-Saharan Africa, where migration desire remains the highest globally, 33% say they would like to move permanently, also a decade low. As recently as 2023, that figure stood at 37%, ticking upward from 36% in 2021-2022.

In regions that are typically on the receiving end of migrants, the picture is different. Migration desire in the United States and Canada (20%) and the European Union (21%) remains near record highs.

In the U.S., notably, the heightened desire to move abroad is concentrated among women younger than 45. In 2025, 40% of U.S. women aged 15 to 44 say they would move permanently to another country if they had the opportunity, up from 10% in 2014. The trend first rose sharply in 2016 and continued across multiple years, suggesting a broader shift in outlook rather than a short-term political effect.

Bottom Line

It is important to note that desire to migrate is not the same as intent to move. Not everyone who wants to move can or will do so. The 2025 data show that fewer people worldwide are imagining their futures elsewhere, and the U.S., long the world’s most desired destination, is attracting less of that interest than at any point in nearly two decades.

For years, the dominant story in global migration data was a rising desire to move across nearly every region. The 2025 data suggest that pattern is shifting. The declines are widespread and concentrated in the regions that have historically driven global migration.

At the same time, the picture is not uniform. In regions that typically receive migrants, including the U.S. and Canada, along with the EU, desire to leave remains near record highs. And within the U.S., a growing number of younger women say they would move abroad permanently if they could.

These patterns show that interest in moving abroad, and to the U.S. in particular, is shifting across regions. But despite these changes, many people worldwide — an estimated 900 million — would like to move, including about 134 million who would prefer to move to the U.S.

Read Gallup’s analysis of how these shifts in migration desire could translate into changes in population size and human capital across countries.

Andrew Dugan and Michelle Chau contributed to this analysis.

item.title: Hello Toronto – Waymo Is En Route (114 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://waymo.com/blog/2026/10/waymo-in-toronto/, See on Hacker News

Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.

In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.

“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”

To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International.

"As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."

As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.

Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others.

“Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults.

We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028.

Au cours des prochains jours, vous commencerez à voir des véhicules Waymo circuler dans les rues de Toronto, avec un conducteur au volant. Notre démarche est rigoureuse et axée avant tout sur la sécurité. Nous procédons par étapes, en commençant par cartographier le réseau routier local en haute définition, puis en effectuant des essais avec des spécialistes qualifiés de la conduite autonome au volant. Cette phase nous permettra de vérifier que le Waymo Driver s’adapte aux conditions de conduite propres à Toronto.

« Notre arrivée au Canada marque une étape importante dans le développement international de Waymo », a déclaré Tekedra Mawakana, codirectrice générale de l’entreprise. « Toronto est l’une des plus grandes métropoles du monde : une ville innovante, diversifiée et résolument tournée vers l’avenir. Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. »

Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Element nous fournira des services complets de gestion de flottes. Avec Element et nos autres partenaires, nous investirons progressivement dans la création de centaines d’emplois liés à l’entretien de la flotte, aux essais sur route, au service à la clientèle et à d’autres activités nécessaires à l’exploitation de notre service. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier.

« En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. »

Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps, pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type.

La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario.

« L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults.

Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

item.title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio (139 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/mlx-distributed-inference, See on Hacker News

content type Featured highlight

MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:

mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.

Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.

Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.

Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.

The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.

While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline

In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).

In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.

It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk kk, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k+1k+1, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.

Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.

With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.

With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.

The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2, the one-cable run being an additional experiment.

Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080

As with mlx_lm.benchmark, the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode, which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
  "provider": {
    "mlx": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Local MLX",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4": {
          "name": "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.

Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.

item.title: I Love Software Rendering (208 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.jamesfmackenzie.com/2026/10/13/i-love-software-rendering/, See on Hacker News

I love software rendering. The best DOS experience I’ve had in a long while was Quake in its software renderer at 800×600, running at a locked 60fps on my Dell OptiPlex 380. It’s one of the best-looking things I’ve seen a DOS game do.

That’s not how most people remember those games looking. In the 90s you either ran them in software at a low resolution, or you bought a 3D card and played the accelerated version. Today there’s a third option: run the software renderer on a machine fast enough to push it at resolutions nobody could use back then.

What software rendering is

In a software-rendered game, the CPU draws every pixel. There’s no 3D card involved: the game works out each frame in its own code and writes it straight to video memory. Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and the original Quake all work this way.

When 3D cards arrived, many games got accelerated versions. GLQuake came after Quake, and Blood and Tomb Raider got 3dfx modes. Those versions hand the drawing to the graphics card, and they look different.

Why I like the look

It’s sharp. Software renderers generally sample textures pixel by pixel, so every texel stays a crisp square. Early 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering, which looked impressive in 1997 but turns everything soft and blurry to my eye now.

It’s gritty. Most of these games ran in 256 colours, with lighting done through lookup tables into that palette. Shadows fall off in visible steps rather than smooth gradients. Technically that’s colour banding, a limitation. In practice it gives the games a rough, grimy texture that I really like, and that hardware rendering smooths away.

It’s how the games were built. Quake was released with its software renderer, and GLQuake followed. Doom and the Build engine games were designed around their software renderers from the start.

It isn’t always the better option. When I got a Voodoo 2 running in a modern PC, Blood ran fast in its 3dfx mode, but the VESA software modes were the better-looking option. Tomb Raider went the other way: its underwater sections look noticeably better accelerated than in the DOS software renderer. So it’s a preference, not a rule. But for most of the games I care about, I’d pick the software renderer.

It’s not just nostalgia, either. Ion Fury, a Build engine game from 2019, still ships with a software renderer.

The catch: it needs a fast PC

Software rendering scales with the CPU. Every extra pixel is work for the processor, so the high VESA resolutions that many late DOS games offered were well beyond the hardware of the day.

Modern hardware can power through most of it. On the OptiPlex 380, Quake at 800×600 holds a locked 60fps. But the heaviest games still push even very fast machines. In his video on the Portwell RUBY-9719, Rasteri shows Build engine games needing far more power at high resolutions, to the point where even a 3.3GHz quad-core Xeon “isn’t quite enough to run Shadow Warrior at full 1600 by 1200”.

So if you want to see these games at their best, you want the fastest machine you can get that still runs them.

Why it needs native DOS

There are other ways to get software rendering on a modern PC. Source ports of Doom and Quake run software renderers on Windows, and Ion Fury runs on Windows natively. They’re great.

What I’m after is the original DOS versions running as they were released, on real hardware. DOSBox is the obvious alternative, but some DOS titles struggle in DOSBox, while on real hardware they behave exactly as intended.

That leaves one more problem: sound. A fast machine running native DOS needs a sound card the games can talk to, and modern PCs don’t have one. That’s a story of its own.

Games worth trying

  • Quake, in software at 800×600 or higher
  • Duke Nukem 3D and Blood, the Build engine games, at high VESA resolutions
  • Screamer

item.title: The Folders Programming Language (182 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://danieltemkin.com/esolangs/folders, See on Hacker News

Created 2015 | Updated 2026 | One of Forty-Four Esolangs, by the creator of Rivulet and Velato

Where directories are code and drive space is infinite

About

Folders is a non-textual language, where code is expressed in containment and order alone. The names of the folders are ignored, apart from alphabetical ordering. In other words, they are pure ordered trees.

Inspired by the Whitespace language, Folders is devoted to the idea of dematerialized code. It began with the question What is more empty than a file with no visible text? The empty folder is clutter, an appendage with no purpose. In git, it is ignored entirely (for this reason, it is suggested that Folders programs put .gitignore files in their deepest reaches).

Folders began as a Windows language. In Windows, folders are an even more extreme measure of emptiness: they take up no disk space at all. For proof, create 352,449 folders and get properties on it. In this way, Folders offers not only a dematerialized approach to code but also infinite storage capacity. Keep all your data encoded in folder names and never worry about running out of space again.

For those who use other operating systems, the emulator below gives some of the experience of how Folders manages data and code.

The original implementation can be found on github.

Encoding

Each command folder has at least one child folder. The number of subfolders in the first folder (alphabetically) indicates the type of command; any arguments are indicated in a second folder; some commands require a third folder. Expressions are the same: the number of folders in the first sub-folder determine what kind of expression it is. The full Language Spec is below.

Temporary data is stored as folders; unlike Folders code, it is the name of the folder that stores the data.

Folders FS

The Folders interpreter does not create temp files; anything not held immediately in memory is stored as a set of temp folders. Unlike Folders code, the name of the folder stores the data itself. The prefered I/O of Folders is another set of folders. This means you can encode all your data in folders, bypassing the "material realm" of files entirely and giving you infinite disk space (attempt at your own risk). Folders lang for code, Folders FS for data storage.

Visualizations

A Folders program is a nil-terminated nested list. Its simplest form is pure containment and order, like this all-array JSON:

That is also how the JS emulator saves/reads Folders programs.

However, other systems of visualization are possible. Folders programs are content as structure and can be applied to raw data of any type. Here is a Truth Machine as a contour map. The thicker lines are containers, and the order of folders is read starting at the upper left (NW corner) and proceeding counter-clockwise.

Other visualizations might be a family tree (with all single parents), a botanical branching structure (like a splitting stalk of wheat), or the paths through a maze.

The red dots indicate a threshhold from a container to a single child.

Language Spec

The language itself is a very simple imperative language with a short list of semantic rules.

For Commands and Expressions, the number of folders in their first child folder determines their use. Types are used directly.

Commands

Command # of Folders Details
if 0 folders Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands
while 1 folder Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands
declare 2 folders Second sub-folder holds type, third holds var name (in number of folders)
let 3 folders Second holds var name (in number of folders), third holds expression
print 4 folders Second sub-folder holds expression
input 5 folders Second sub-folder holds var name

Expressions

Type # of Folders Details
variable 0 folders Second sub-folder holds var name
add 1 folder Second sub-folder holds first expression to add, third holds second expression
subtract 2 folders Second sub-folder holds first expression to subtract, third holds second expression
multiply 3 folders Second sub-folder holds first expression to multiply, third holds second expression
divide 4 folders Second sub-folder holds first expression to divide, third holds second expression
literal value 5 folders Second sub-folder holds the type of the value (e.g. two folders for a string, third holds the value)
equal to 6 folders Second and third folders hold expressions to compare
greater than 7 folders Second and third folders hold expressions to compare
less than 8 folders Second and third folders hold expressions to compare

Types

Type # of Folders
float 1 folder
string 2 folders
char 3 folders
The reference compiler on github: https://github.com/rottytooth/Folders

item.title: Any window from your Mac, on your iPhone and iPad (227 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/Saffsanity/sill, See on Hacker News

Any window from your Mac, on your iPhone and iPad.

Sill shows a window from your Mac, or the whole desktop, on your iPhone or iPad. You use it there with touch, a trackpad, a keyboard or Apple Pencil. Sill for Mac captures the window, encodes it as HEVC video and sends it to the Sill app on your device. Your taps, clicks, scrolls and keys go back to your Mac. Your Mac and your device connect on the same network, over a USB cable, with Direct Wireless Connection when they share no network, or through your own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access. There is no account and no server in between.

getsill.app · Download for Mac · Support · Privacy · Terms

Sill for Mac is a free, notarized download from getsill.app; with Homebrew, brew install --cask saffsanity/sill/sill installs the same download from Sill's own tap. Sill for iPhone and iPad is free on the App Store, and you can also build it from source (below).

Screenshots

These are the iPad screenshots from the App Store; on iPhone and iPhone Duo, Sill has layouts of its own.

Requirements

  • A Mac with Apple silicon, on macOS 14 or later.
  • An iPhone or iPad with iOS 17 or iPadOS 17 or later.
  • On your Mac, Sill asks for Screen Recording, to show your windows, and Accessibility, to click, scroll and type for you and to move and size the window it shows. On macOS 15 or later, also allow Local Network. On your iPhone or iPad, Sill asks for Local Network, to find your Mac, and for the camera when you scan your Mac's pairing code (you can type the code instead).
  • Your Mac and your device on the same network, joined by a USB cable, or near each other with Direct Wireless Connection on. Away from home, your own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access on.

How it works

  • Sill for Mac lives in the menu bar. When your device picks a window, or the whole desktop, Sill captures it with ScreenCaptureKit and encodes it as HEVC with VideoToolbox, on the hardware video encoder in your Mac (or, while that is busy, in software). It captures nothing while no device is connected.
  • The picture goes over an encrypted connection (TLS 1.3) straight to the Sill app on your iPhone or iPad, which decodes and shows it. When the encoder or the link falls behind, Sill drops frames rather than queue them, so the picture stays current.
  • Your input goes back the same way: taps and clicks, scrolls with momentum, the on-screen trackpad, keys and typed text, and Apple Pencil as the pointer. Sill for Mac turns it into mouse and keyboard events, which needs Accessibility. A keyboard attached to your device types on your Mac as soon as the picture shows, Esc included, and a trackpad or a mouse scrolls the window under its pointer. Three fingers swipe and pinch as on a Mac's trackpad: Mission Control, App Exposé, the Spaces, Apps and Show Desktop, through the keyboard shortcuts your Mac has for them.
  • On iPhone, held upright, the picture is on top with buttons, keys and a trackpad below. Larger Picture, in the settings panel, gives a window's picture the room of the window thumbnails, down to where the keyboard comes up; the Desktop keeps the usual layout. A window keeps its own shape until you set its text size with Aa, or turn on the virtual display; then your Mac makes it fill the taller picture.
  • The clipboard goes both ways while Share Clipboard is on, in both apps: text you copy on your Mac is ready to paste on your device, and Paste in Sill sends what you copied on your device to your Mac's clipboard, where you press ⌘V. Sill never reads your device's clipboard by itself, and copies a password manager marks as concealed stay on your Mac.
  • On iPhone Duo, Sill follows the hinge: open it flat and your Mac fills the inner display; half open, the picture is above the fold with a trackpad and keys below; closed, Sill runs on the cover display. Nothing you touch sits on the fold.
  • The menus of the app you use reach your device too: in the iPad's own menu bar on iPadOS 26 or later, and behind the Menus button in Sill's bar. Sill for Mac reads each menu from the app as you open it and chooses the item you pick, through Accessibility. When someone moves the mouse at your Mac, your device shows the pointer where it is.
  • Nearby, your device finds your Mac with Bonjour on your local network. Over a USB cable, your Mac shows as Wired and the connection uses the cable. With no shared network, Direct Wireless Connection (off by default) connects over peer-to-peer Wi-Fi, the way AirDrop does.
  • Pairing: you pair each iPhone or iPad with your Mac once. Tap your Mac on the device, and your Mac shows a code: scan it, or type its 12 digits. Over a USB cable the device pairs by itself. From then on each end knows the other's key, and every connection, nearby or away, is pinned to those keys. In Sill's Settings on your Mac, Devices lists the devices you paired, and you can remove any of them there.
  • Away from home, Remote Access (off by default) lets the devices you paired reach your Mac through your own VPN or a port you forward on your router; a device learns how the next time it connects at home with Remote Access on. A device away from home gets a quality of its own, Low at Standard resolution until you pick another there or in Sill's settings, so a slow connection never starts at your home quality; your home quality comes back as soon as a device at home connects. When your device comes home and your network lists your Mac, the session moves to your network by itself.
  • When the link can't keep up, Sill for Mac notices that it is holding frames back and tells your device, which says so over the picture and, in its Settings, offers a quality the link can carry.
  • Text size: Aa on your device resizes the window you stream on your Mac, through Accessibility, so its text shows at the size you pick, and keeps it at that size while it streams. The window goes back to its own size and place when Sill stops showing it: you pick another window or the Desktop, your last device disconnects, or you quit Sill. If you moved it on your Mac meanwhile, it keeps its new place.
  • The virtual display (off by default) moves a window you stream onto a display of its own on your Mac, so it keeps updating when other windows cover it. It uses a private macOS API, which is one reason Sill for Mac comes from the website and not from the Mac App Store.

Good to know: Sill shows one window, or the whole desktop, at a time, and it does not play sound from your Mac. The clipboard carries text only, up to 256 KB at a time, and only between apps that both have it. Your Mac needs to be awake, with Sill open. Sill may not be able to wake it. After a restart Sill opens only once someone logs in, with Launch at Login on. Only the iPhones and iPads you paired can connect, unless you turn off Require pairing in Settings › Devices; then any device on your network can, still encrypted. Pairing at home came with Sill for Mac 0.4.0 and Sill for iPhone and iPad 0.5 (2), and each needs the other: the iPhone and iPad app shows an older Sill for Mac as "Update Sill", and an older iPhone and iPad app can't connect to Sill for Mac 0.4.0 or later at home. Since 0.5.1 the two apps share one version number for each release. With Sill for Mac 0.3.1 or earlier, connections on your local network, over the cable and over Direct Wireless Connection are not encrypted, and anything that reaches your Mac there can connect without pairing: update it.

Tips

Sill is free, with no ads, no tracking and no subscription. If it is useful to you, a tip through GitHub Sponsors helps pay for the developer account. A tip unlocks nothing: every feature is free.

Building from source

You need a Mac with Xcode (Sill is built with Xcode 27; the iPhone and iPad app needs Xcode 27.1 or later, for the iPhone Duo's hinge and fold), selected as the active developer directory, with its license accepted.

Sill for Mac, from the repository's folder:

Scripts/make-app.sh --install --open

This builds Sill.app with SwiftPM, signs it with your Apple Development identity, replaces /Applications/Sill.app and opens it. If that was the Sill for Mac you downloaded, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility again and pair each device again: the download keeps its key and paired devices in the data-protection keychain, which only a Developer ID build with the project's provisioning profile reads, and a build of your own keeps them in your login keychain. Without --install it only builds .build/Sill.app. With no Apple Development identity it signs ad hoc, and then Screen Recording and Accessibility have to be granted again after every build.

For work on the host itself, swift run -c release SillHost runs the same host on the command line, with one difference: unless you add --pairing, its home door is plain and open, with no pairing and no encryption, and any device on your network can connect to it, so run it only while developing. The App Store's Sill for iPhone and iPad never dials such a door ("Update Sill"); a Debug build from this repository can (docs/DEVELOPMENT.md, Pairing at home). With --synthetic it streams a test pattern with no Screen Recording needed.

The iPhone and iPad app:

  1. Open iOSClient/Sill.xcodeproj.
  2. In the Sill target's Signing & Capabilities, pick your team, and change the bundle identifier me.saffer.sill to one of your own.
  3. Run it on an iPhone or iPad on the same network as your Mac, and tap your Mac. The first time, a Sill for Mac built from this repository asks you to pair: scan the code it shows, or connect the device with a USB cable.

docs/DEVELOPMENT.md has the rest: every command-line flag, the test tools and the simulator harness, permissions and how to reset them, Remote Access, troubleshooting and releases.

Contributing

Issues are welcome: bug reports, questions and ideas. For a pull request, keep to the conventions and decisions in CLAUDE.md: Swift and Apple frameworks only, no third-party dependencies, nothing that needs a server, and latency before picture quality. Open an issue before starting anything large. Before a pull request, Tests/checks/run-all.sh runs the same pure checks as CI, in about five minutes and with no device. Contributions are accepted under the project's license. Please report a security problem privately, as SECURITY.md says, not in a public issue.

License

item.title: Thank You, Deno (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.vlt.io/blog/competition-keeps-javascript-moving, See on Hacker News

All Posts

open sourceregistry

Deno is joining Cloudflare & winding down its investment in the runtime. We're all better off because of its existence.

Ryan Dahl announced last week that the Deno team is joining Cloudflare. The Deno runtime winds down over the next year, JSR keeps running on Cloudflare's infrastructure, & the team's new job, per Cloudflare's post, is merging Deno's celld into workerd.

The announcement came two years to the day after Deno 2 shipped. Bun joined Anthropic ten months ago. The tempting conclusion is that the alternative-runtime experiment is over & Node has won by default. In reality, the ecosystem has gotten the benefits Deno was pushing, just not from Deno itself.

Competition is imperative to a healthy ecosystem

Unfortunately, Deno never really hit critical mass in production; Node is as dominant in 2026 as it was in 2018. What Deno did achieve was to reinvigorate & put pressure on the incumbent, & that pressure didn't only run one way.

Deno started as a clean break. Ryan stood up at JSConf EU in 2018 & listed what he'd do differently from Node: deny-by-default permissions, TypeScript as a first-class input, web-standard APIs on the server, ES modules only, a single executable. And, pointedly, no npm, no package.json & no node_modules. Dependencies were URLs. The slides put it plainly: "There is no need to list dependencies."

A lot of us who'd spent years on npm & Node were skeptical of that last part (not the permissions or the TypeScript, which were obviously good) & said so at the time. We'd been there before, in the hotlinking era, when every page pulled jquery.min.js off somebody else's server & broke when it moved or got compromised. A URL tells you where something was, not what it is. Once you care that the bytes you tested are the bytes you ship, you need an integrity hash & somewhere to record it, & you've reinvented the lockfile. Matteo Collina of the Node TSC said in 2020 that "another left-pad incident is waiting to happen, but this time there is no 'central entity' that can fix it." Some of this skepticism was defensive but happened to be right in the end.

Deno 1.0 shipped in 2020 on the original terms, & then spent the next four years walking them back one piece at a time. First the deps.ts convention, one file that re-exported every URL: a manifest in all but name. Then lock.json, an integrity hash per URL: a lockfile. Then import maps, so you could write bare specifiers again. Deno's own documentation today recommends registries over HTTPS imports because they "can drift to different versions across files" & "trust the serving host." Those were the objections from 2018, restated as guidance.

Then Bun showed up. Bun 0.1 was released in July 2022 with the opposite bet: rebuild the toolchain from scratch for speed, but run existing npm packages, read package.json & act as a drop-in replacement for node. About six weeks later, Deno published "Big Changes Ahead for Deno", announcing npm: specifiers, a commitment to make 80–90% of npm packages work within three months & a new goal of being "the fastest JavaScript runtime." Deno credited user feedback for the shift; the timing suggests Bun was a large part of it. Deno 2, in October 2024, finished the job with full Node & npm compatibility. Four years after launching as the alternative to Node's ecosystem, Deno had become another way to run it.

That was the right call, & it was also an admission that the ecosystem wasn't going to abandon over a decade's worth of dependencies overnight. Cloudflare's workerd, which it open-sourced in 2022, grew its own Node compatibility layer for the same reason: that's where the packages are.

Node ended up needing to respond. Since 2018 it has shipped a global fetch, WebSocket, Web Streams & Web Crypto; a stable test runner & --watch; --env-file & single-executable builds; a stable permission model; type stripping on by default; node:sqlite; & require(esm). Node's contributors (many volunteers) did the hard work to listen & make big changes, & they deserve a ton of credit for it, but I don't think it happens on that timeline without three other runtimes shipping many of these ideas first. A mature open source project rarely lacks good ideas. It lacks urgency, & competitors supply that urgency.

The standards work came out of the same pressure: WinterCG formed in 2022 because several serious runtimes made "what's the minimum common API?" a practical question, & now, as Ecma TC55, it should outlast whichever runtimes consolidate next.

Package managers & registries

For most of its history the JavaScript package ecosystem was a monoculture: one client, one registry, & an API contract informal enough that it stayed effectively undocumented for a decade & a half. Nearly every improvement since came from someone refusing to accept the status quo.

Yarn (2016) insisted installs be deterministic & gave us the lockfile, workspaces & an offline cache; npm 5 shipped package-lock.json the next year. pnpm showed that node_modules didn't have to be hundreds of megabytes of duplicated files. Bun made install fast enough that the incumbents had to revisit their performance. Deno argued you should be able to read a dependency's source before you take it, & while URL imports didn't last, that idea did.

The clearest recent example is install scripts. pnpm & Bun stopped running them by default; vlt never did. The argument had been made inside npm for the entire time I worked there without ever becoming the default. In June of this year, after a run of supply-chain worms, GitHub announced that npm 12 would stop running them by default too. Nothing about the idea changed in those years; enough other package managers shipped it that npm could no longer treat it as radical. The pressure runs in both directions too: we borrowed catalogs from pnpm, & pnpm's namedRegistries borrowed our named-registry aliases.

On the registry side, JSR deserves credit. It made a different set of bets than we did: publish TypeScript source, require ESM, generate docs from code. We disagreed with parts of it & added jsr: support to vlt anyway because our users asked for it. It survives the wind-down because, as far as I can tell, it's cheap to run, its API is documented, & Cloudflare had a reason to keep it alive.

What changes now

The two most popular independent, venture-backed JavaScript runtimes now live inside companies whose business is something else. Jarred Sumner said the Bun team's relationship with the Claude Code team "probably will look similar to the relationship between Google Chrome <> V8," with more independence, & Cloudflare's post makes clear that workerd's roadmap is Cloudflare's. That's how JavaScriptCore & V8 have always been funded, & it's still a change.

Whether a community fork of the Deno runtime emerges will tell us whether the ecosystem values a secure-by-default, standards-first runtime enough to pay for one that isn't attached to a cloud. And celld-into-workerd is new optionality at a layer that has had very little: a self-hostable, open implementation of Workers & Durable Objects, led by Ryan & Bert Belder.

JavaScript has insurance at almost every layer: three production engines, several runtimes, several package managers. When one layer consolidates, as the runtime layer is doing now, the others hold. The churn that makes this possible is also what people complain about most. "JavaScript fatigue" has been a running joke for a decade: a new framework every week, a new bundler every month, & yet another package manager, which, yes, I'm aware I've contributed to. But nobody had to leave Node to get fetch, a permission model or TypeScript without a build step, & nobody has to switch package managers to get install scripts turned off by default anymore. Those things showed up in the tools people were already using because someone else shipped them first & the incumbent had to answer. The projects didn't always win, but the ideas usually did, & end-users collected them either way.

To Ryan, Bert, Bartek & the rest of the Deno team (past & present): your collective efforts have enriched our shared ecosystem. Thank you!

Darcy Clarke
Founder & CEO, vlt

item.title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes (213 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ipinfo.io/blog/rpki-protects-70-internet-routes, See on Hacker News

The Internet relies on networks telling each other which IP addresses they can deliver traffic to, using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol). These routing announcements have historically depended heavily on trust. When a network announces addresses it shouldn’t, accidentally or deliberately, traffic can be sent to the wrong place and services can become unreachable.

On February 24, 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing a more specific route for YouTube's addresses. Its upstream provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), accepted the announcement and passed it to the rest of the Internet, redirecting YouTube traffic to Pakistan globally for roughly two hours (RIPE NCC's case study). That’s exactly the kind of error RPKI is designed to prevent. Work on RPKI had started at the IETF two years earlier, and the regional Internet registries began issuing RPKI certificates in 2011.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) lets the holder of a block of IP addresses publish a signed record, a Route Origin Authorization (ROA), naming the networks (Autonomous Systems, or ASes) allowed to announce it. Network operators that check RPKI compare announcements against those records and can reject the ones that fail.

The share of routed prefixes (blocks of IP addresses) that are RPKI-valid rose from 54.0% in September 2025 to 70.3% in September 2026, a gain of 16.4 percentage points, or 30% in a year. That’s a sharp increase. In each of the two years before, it rose three to four points. Much of the jump came from one country: China went from 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes to 83.0%, almost 60% of the global gain counted by addresses.

RPKI is doing what it was designed to do. A typical valid prefix is seen by 596 of the routers that feed the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors. One with no RPKI record is seen by 595, and an invalid one by just two. 

Invalid Routes Barely Propagate

In August, the Internet Society Pulse found RPKI-related activity accounts for under 1% of daily BGP update volume, a share that is rising but still small, so RPKI is not itself destabilizing routing. We wanted to know whether RPKI was actually protecting Internet routing.

Routes with an RPKI record and routes with none travel equally far: a typical one is seen by 596 and 595 vantage points. Routes that fail the check are seen by just two. Now that enough networks check, they are dropping these invalid routes. Nearly half of all invalid routes reach only a single vantage point. When the wrong network announces the addresses, the clearest kind of hijack or mistake, 71% reach only one.

This changes how country-level RPKI statistics should be read. A country can look bad because of announcements almost nobody sees.

Simply counting invalid routes can badly exaggerate how much of a country is affected. Spain has the highest share of invalid IPv4 prefixes at 28.2%. Count the addresses in those routes instead, weighted by how many vantage points see each one, and it falls to 0.057%. Slovakia falls from 17.4% to almost zero. Italy has the highest figure of any country with at least a million IPv4 addresses, 0.121%, up from 0.075% a year ago, and 90% of it is one network. 

WIND TRE (AS1267) announces 34 routes in its own address space that its own ROAs don't allow: 19 are more specific than the ROAs permit, and 15 come from AS1267 while the ROA names WIND TRE's other network, AS24608. None reaches more than 77 vantage points, against about 617 for the signed blocks around them.

China Drove Most of the 2026 Jump

Counted by IPv4 addresses on September 28 each year, the share in RPKI-valid routes rose from 42.7% in 2023 to 47.9% in 2024, 53.1% in 2025 and 65.0% in 2026. The last jump was 11.9 points, against about five in each previous year.

Removing China shows how much of that was one country. Outside China, the share rose from 58.0% to 63.2%, a 5.2-point gain, a little less than the year before.

China's own change was extraordinary. 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses were in valid routes in September 2025, and 83.0% a year later. Most of that happened this year: at the end of December 2025, just 2.9% of China's routed prefixes were valid. It also changed which way it moves the world figure. In 2025 China pulled the global average down: 53.1% worldwide against 58.0% without China. In 2026 it pushed it up: 65.0% against 63.2%. Others moved a long way too: Egypt from 23% to 99%, Kazakhstan from 16% to 84%, Mexico from 37% to 78%, and South Africa from 38% to 60%.

Where the unprotected addresses are is just as concentrated. Of all routed IPv4 space not in RPKI-valid routes on September 28, nearly 60% is in the United States, and about one in four addresses belongs to the US Department of Defense (more on who holds IPv4 in an upcoming post). Most of that is space the Department began announcing in 2021 to watch for misuse, not to run services.

IPv6 Has Moved Ahead

In early 2025 there were concerns that IPv6 adoption of RPKI was slowing. Instead, it accelerated and has now overtaken IPv4. In RPKI's 2024 year in review for RIPE Labs, Job Snijders noted IPv6 ROA growth "seems to be stalling." Over our window, IPv6 routed prefixes marked valid rose from 56% to 79% while IPv4 prefixes rose from 54% to 68%, putting IPv6 roughly ten points ahead. The Hurricane Electric RPKI report shows the same ordering.

Two other metrics he flagged also changed: the average number of address blocks per ROA climbed back from 2.31 at the end of December to 2.62, and publication points, which he counted falling from 63 to 53 and read as consolidation, rose from 73 to 91 as more organizations began hosting their own repositories instead of relying on their registry.

What RPKI Does Not Do

RPKI validates who may originate a prefix. It does not validate the path, and it cannot catch an attacker who stays inside the permission you published, so it's not bulletproof.

On August 28, 2026, a route for 162.55.80.0/24 (a block of 256 addresses) appeared with Hetzner's AS24940 forged as the origin. Hetzner's ROA covered the surrounding /16, a block 256 times larger, and allowed announcements as small as a /24, so the forged route satisfied it. The route was RPKI-valid, no legitimate /24 existed to compete with it, and longest-prefix-match meant everyone preferred it. That was enough to obtain a genuine TLS certificate and serve a malicious Virtualizor update to hypervisors, as documented by Kentik. Nothing about RPKI failed. The ROA permitted it.

We measured how common that posture is. Of 855,217 RPKI-covered IPv4 routes, 138,698, or 16.2%, have a ROA looser than the route announced and no more-specific route of their own filling the gap. For IPv6 it is 20.9%. That leaves roughly 18 million more-specific prefixes an attacker could announce today, forge the origin, and come out RPKI-valid and uncontested.

Operators in the same business make very different choices here. Among hosting providers, Contabo has an open window on 540 of 553 covered routes and DigitalOcean on 780 of 863, while OVH sits at 11.5%. Access providers are worse still: Cablevision at 98.1%, Shaw at 96.5%, Bharti Airtel at 85.0%.

RFC 9319 already says the best practice is to leave maxLength unset. maxLength is the setting that lets a ROA also cover smaller blocks inside it, so leaving it unset means a ROA matches only the block actually announced. Hetzner tightened three prefixes after the incident, including the one that was hijacked, though 49 of its 63 covered routes remain open.

Where RPKI Coverage Declined

RPKI coverage can also disappear without causing an outage. A missing ROA simply removes the protection, and nobody notices unless they look. We found several cases where that happened over the past year.

Unlike China, Mauritius saw its RPKI coverage fall. The share of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes fell from 94.0% to 69.0% between September 2025 and September 2026. SEACOM (AS37100) lost four of its six ROAs on January 1. One covered 105.16.0.0/12, a block of about a million addresses, 46% of which are in Mauritius. That block alone explains Mauritius's drop, and it still had no ROA on September 28.

Two other operators show the same thing happening and then being fixed. Saudi Telecom (AS25019) lost RPKI protection on 19 routes, including six large blocks totaling about 1.6 million addresses, when the ROAs for those six blocks disappeared between March 30 and April 13. Saudi Arabia's coverage recovered when the ROAs came back on September 21 and 22. 

In Morocco, Orange Maroc (AS36925) is the only large operator that publishes ROAs, and most of them went missing twice: from July 2025 to July 2026, and again from July 25 to September 3. Morocco went from 20% covered to almost none, and back.

One Measurement Trap

There is a critical measurement trap here. Some validation methods can count an RPKI record as failed even though it is still providing protection in practice.

Every signed record carries a link to the certificate above it. When an operator moves its repository, that link can go stale, and a check that inspects records one by one will report a hard failure. But the validation that actually produces the list routers use never follows that link, it walks down from the trust anchors instead. 

We found thousands of records flagged as failed that were present in every independently validated set we checked, with their routes still RPKI-valid. So if you are reading anyone's RPKI numbers, including ours, it is worth knowing which of the two they counted. A count of failing records is not a measure of lost protection.

Path Validation Is Starting to Arrive

ROAs secure the origin of a route. They say nothing about whether the path used to reach that origin makes sense.

ASPA, or Autonomous System Provider Authorization, addresses that. A network publishes a signed record naming its authorized upstream providers, which lets others check observed AS paths against them and catch route leaks that origin validation misses.

Deployment is early but fast. On September 28, 2025, 131 networks had published ASPA records. By September 28, 2026 there were 3,272, 25 times as many.

The growth comes in steps rather than a curve. RIPE NCC sat at about 85 networks from September to late November, then climbed to 470 by the end of December. ARIN stepped up from January 21, APNIC at the end of June and again in September, when its count nearly doubled. Each jump follows a registry making ASPA signing available, so tooling has been the main driver. One detail: APNIC announced its support on July 9, and its curve started climbing on June 26.

That coverage is now enough to ask the better question: how much of observed routing is ASPA-valid?

On September 28, 2026, 9.7% of observed routing passed ASPA checks, up from 6.2% a year earlier. Most of that is automatic: under the draft rules, a path through only one or two networks always passes, and those short paths were about 6% of routing in both years.

Take them out and the records networks have published verify about 3.5% of routing, up from roughly 0.1%. That is the real progress.

Almost all the rest is not failing. It is unknown, because too few networks along those paths have published records to tell. In practice, ASPA can check only a small slice of routing today, and that slice grows with every network that publishes a record.

More interesting is the part that can be judged and fails. Paths breaking ASPA's rules mid-path, the signal a collector can read with most confidence, rose from effectively zero to 0.048% of observations. That is not necessarily routing getting worse: a path can only be called invalid once enough of it has declared providers, so as publication grew, paths that were previously unjudgeable became testable and some failed.

Attributing those failures needs care, because the gap sits mid-path: one provider with a stale record makes every one of its customers' routes look invalid, so ranking by origin blames the wrong party.

Attribute to the hop instead and the networks at the top are the ones doing it right. Cogent, Arelion, and GTT each declare AS0, which says they buy transit from nobody. That is true, and it is exactly what stops a stale record further down the path from hiding as "no attestation." The real gaps are smaller: of 3,272 networks publishing ASPA records, 479 have upstream providers visible in our routing data that they never declared, across 658 missing relationships.

The largest single cause is one operator. Syrian Telecom (AS29386) publishes a record naming four carriers. Three of them carry just 16% of the transit we observe through it, and the fourth carries none. The four carriers that handle the other 84% are missing from the record, so about 40% of paths arriving through them fail the check, and the rest come out unknown. 

Through Syrian Telecom's own routes and those of two Syrian networks that reach the Internet through it, that record accounts for 21% of all mid-path ASPA failures on the Internet. Another 3 points come from AS201550, a second Syrian Telecom network whose record copies the same four carriers instead of naming the Syrian Telecom networks it connects through. Which means the global ASPA failure rate is not yet a measure of the Internet's health. About a quarter of it comes from one operator's incomplete records.

Eighteen years after PCCW Global passed on Pakistan Telecom's announcement for YouTube's addresses, PCCW is a gap in the newer system. ASPA would not have stopped the 2008 incident; RPKI's origin check is what covers that. But ASPA lets others check PCCW's place in a path, and AS3491 has not published a record. That breaks nothing on its own. Still, nearly 6,000 paths crossing PCCW read ASPA-invalid today, because networks below it publish records that leave PCCW out.

What Operators Can Do

RPKI now protects most Internet routes, and invalid routes barely travel. The gaps that remain are mostly in the hands of the networks that own the addresses:

  • Publish ROAs for everything you announce. Three in ten routed prefixes are still not RPKI-valid.
  • Leave maxLength unset. One in six covered IPv4 routes has a window like the one used against Hetzner.
  • Check that your ROAs are still there. Saudi Telecom, SEACOM, and Orange Maroc each lost some of theirs, and since nothing broke, it was easy to miss.
  • Publish ASPA, and list every provider. Syrian Telecom's record leaves out the four carriers that handle most of the traffic we see reaching it, so many routes through them fail the check.

IPinfo tracks the RPKI status of every routed prefix daily: ipinfo.io/data/rpki.

Methodology: All figures come from IPinfo's routing and RPKI datasets, one RPKI snapshot per day. RPKI validity is the share of routed prefixes classified valid against the validated authorization set, not the validation status of individual RPKI objects. Routing data comes from the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors, which IPinfo ingests daily. A prefix's visibility is the number of distinct BGP peers of those collectors carrying it. Across every prefix seen by at least one of them the figure was 70.3% on September 28, 2026; requiring two or more removes isolated announcements and gives 71.4%. Propagation figures are medians; the corresponding means are 519, 515 and 9, pulled up by a tail of more widely seen invalids.

Country figures use IPv4 only and count addresses, not prefixes. Each routed prefix is split across countries by IPinfo geolocation, so a /16 with half its addresses in Italy counts 32,768 addresses toward Italy. Where routes overlap, each address is counted once, and current geolocation is used for every year. An address counts as covered if any RPKI-valid route includes it. The prefix share in Chart 3 assigns each prefix to the country of its first address. The weighted invalid share in Chart 3 is counted per route: it multiplies each route's addresses by the number of vantage points that see it.

Propagation-weighted figures begin in 2024, as the underlying peer data does not exist for earlier snapshots. Yearly comparisons use September 28 snapshots unless another period is stated.

Figures are single-day snapshots rather than averages. The daily series is stable enough that this makes no practical difference: RPKI-valid share moves a median of 0.05 points a day, and a seven-day mean around each date differs from the single-day value by less than 0.1 points.

The maxLength measurement covers prefixes seen by two or more vantage points on September 28, 2026, which drops isolated announcements. An "open window" is a routed prefix whose covering ROA permits a longer prefix than the one announced, with no more-specific route of the operator's own inside that range.

ASPA figures cover daily observations from September 9, 2025 to September 28, 2026, weighted by route observations rather than distinct AS paths. The 0.048% figure is mid-path invalidity only; terminal-hop invalidity is excluded because it turns on the collector peer's own record, and a single incomplete record there taints that peer's entire table. Two peers account for 70% of it.
