What I Self-Host, What I Don’t, and Why

I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV, then XBMC (later known as Kodi).

Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.

So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin. Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.

Rules

I have a few ground rules.

With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service.

I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There’s no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.

Related, I don’t do Docker anymore. It’s not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I’m already using systemd, and at this point Podman’s integration with systemd is excellent.

Hardware

Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.

My comment on Hacker News about what I self-host prompted some questions about how all of this could run on 16 GB RAM. As I describe below, there are some choices I’ve made that reduce resource demand on my server, but ultimately it turns out you don’t need much hardware to run a lot of stuff. Obviously I’m not running any local inference on this hardware, but for everything non-AI, it has just worked out of the box, or with some simple configuration tweaks.

Services

In alphabetical order.

Actual Budget

Budgeting software with desktop clients and a web application, custom reports, and rules-based categorization. I only use this for budgeting and checking/savings/credit accounts. For tracking investment accounts, I use a cloud service. Some day I’ll try to move away from the latter…

While Actual Budget supports automatic transaction import from various banks, I don’t use this feature. Instead, after each month end, I download the prior month’s transactions (OFX format preferred, CSV if no other option) and import them manually. This works for me because I primarily use Actual Budget for expense tracking, not… actual… budgeting.

Podman.

Audiobookshelf

Add, download and store audiobooks and podcasts on your server, listen to them on your phone. I haven’t used the audiobook feature much, I set it up more for my kids, but it has very nice chapter handling. In the past for podcasts I used PlayerFM, then Pocket Casts, but now unless I’m out of the house without VPN connectivity, I use Audiobookshelf.

Native.

Automatic Ripping Machine (ARM)

ARM automates ripping and transcoding DVDs (and Blu-rays, but I don’t do those). Yes, it’s 2026 and I still rip DVDs. Remember, we cut the cord, so not only is this a conduit for new-to-us content, but it’s also a way for us to get bilingual content (English and French).

Podman.

Backrest

Web UI for Restic backup software. Backups are important! Especially for Immich (photos). Restic does a good job deduplicating and compressing backed up data, and Backrest makes it easy to manage the storage retention policies. Notifications in case of failure go to Gotify.

Native.

Beszel

Beszel is a simple monitoring dashboard that collects basic stats from agents (in the old-fashioned sense of a small background service) to display CPU load, memory and disk usage, temperature, battery, etc. Helps me keep an eye on various other hosts I have around the house (several Rapsberry Pis and a Proxmox cluster that may be the subject of a future post).

Native.

Caddy

Caddy is a web server and reverse proxy. Early on I didn’t understand the value of a reverse proxy, and I thought I would be fine accessing my services with a local DNS name, or even IP address, and port number. But then I started adding more and more services, and some required HTTPS. So I got a domain name (not this one) and set up Caddy to automatically obtain LetsEncrypt SSL certificates, and now nearly all of my services are accessible on my LAN (or over VPN) with HTTPS and friendly subdomain names. Adding a new service is a quick edit to the Caddyfile.

Native.

Cockpit

Cockpit is a web-based admin console for the server. It uses normal system authentication methods. For me, it’s mainly useful for spotting failed services when no notifications are set up for them.

Native.

Forgejo

Forgejo is a fork of Gitea, and deploys as a single binary. Github’s uptime is the butt of a lot of jokes these days, but I also appreciate the speed of having my own git remote. Eventually I’ll set up CI/CD and runners, if only to deploy this blog.

Native.

Web-based RSS reader. These days I basically visit two websites, though, so I’ve not been using it much. I do subscribe to the Github releases of some of the services I self-host so I can check out the features and bugfixes in new versions.

Native.

Frigate

Network video recorder (NVR). I first started with Zoneminder because I’m of a certain age. But it became clear that Zoneminder is past its prime. Frigate has been fantastic. I run it with 8 IP cameras. It provides alerts for people and cars entering the driveway, integrates with Home Assistant to power various automations (e.g., when a person is detected in the backyard, turn on the camera floodlight). I may write a future post with some details about my IP camera adventures.

I run all of my cameras at lower resolutions than they support, primarily to avoid Wi-Fi network congestion. Most cameras also support an even lower-resolution RTSP substream, which is what Frigate uses for motion and object detection. Keeping the camera resolutions low avoids excessive CPU and memory from video processing, and excessive disk usage from recordings. They are good enough to identify faces, and privacy laws in my country prohibit filming public rights of way, so my cameras are not aimed at distant points.

Podman.

Gonic

Subsonic-compatible server written in Go. I purchased a perpetual Subsonic license a long time ago, but the original project is ancient and the modern alternatives are better. I run two separate instances of Gonic, one serves kid music, the other serves adult music.

Native.

Gotify

Simple notification service written in Go. Many self-hosted services directly support Gotify notifications, or can send them via a custom HTTP POST. In conjunction with Uptime Kuma, I use Gotify to get notifications about any services or devices that are down, what my kids are watching on Jellyfin, when a new podcast episode is available in Audiobookshelf, etc.

Native.

Home Assistant

Home Assistant probably deserves its own post. It’s fantastic, and I cannot imagine trying to accomplish the same things within a proprietary ecosystem like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, or Apple Home. Things are better now that device manufacturers are standardizing on protocols like Matter, but the control and flexibility you get with Home Assistant is hard to beat. It has a steep learning curve, though, and I need to think about realistic ways to handle potential server failure without compromising the functionality of my home.

Podman.

Homepage

At some point I realized I was running so many services, I needed another service just to keep track of them all. Homepage was a good solution. It has widgets for almost all the services I run, so I can get a quick overview of what’s going on, or just a quick link to the subdomain of a service.

Podman.

Immich

Google Photos alternative. I was tired of Google constantly promoting paid storage plans in their apps. I was able to manage my storage space, but my wife was always about to run out of room. We moved to Immich last year, just after version 2 was released. It’s much faster to load pages full of photos when all the network activity is within your house. I’ve come up with a solution for sharing albums with family, as well. Still a lot of work to do with Immich - I have many duplicates, and now that storage isn’t a concern, I’ve been less disciplined about culling photos and videos.

Podman.

Jellyfin

As I mentioned in the introduction, I’ve self-hosted media for a long time, going all the way back to MythTV twenty-some years ago. Jellyfin is opinionated about its media organization, but it generally works well. I only use it for movies, TV, and home videos, so I can’t speak to its other features (e-books, music, photos, etc.). While my son still remembers Netflix, he is satisfied with Jellyfin. I appreciate the lack of auto-play, never seeing recommendations, and not having to scroll past a bunch of garbage to find what I want to watch.

One of my ways of managing resource demand is by generally preferring 720p media over 1080p or higher. And obviously when ripping DVDs, it’s either 576p or 480p. I do have a 4k TV, but it’s not extremely large, and while I can tell the difference in resolution between SD and HD, for almost everything, 720p seems to be good enough for me.

Podman.

Music Player Daemon (MPD)

Sometimes there are solutions that just work, and don’t really need to change. I think MPD is one of these. It’s been around for 23 years. While Gonic is great for listening to music on my phone, even streaming music from home to my phone while I’m away via VPN, MPD is how I play music through Snapcast to the whole house audio system. I run two instances of MPD, one for music, and one for podcasts.

Native.

PocketBase

I used to keep track of transactions and receipts for special accounts (HSA, 529, etc.) in a SQLite file I accessed directly with SQL Workbench/J. But things became more complicated as I moved between countries, currencies, and different insurance systems, and also wanted to offer my wife the ability to enter transactions. I migrated to PocketBase, which is ultimately still just a SQLite file, but with a nice web-based management frontend that I abuse as a generic CRUD frontend. It’s simple enough for my wife to use as well, and I can still run arbitrary queries against the underlying database file.

Native.

Readeck

Readeck lets me tag and archive copies of stuff I read. I was a heavy Zotero user in graduate school, but I’ve not needed to write a bibliography in years. However, I still read things that I want to ensure I can access later. I tried Wallabag first, but it had trouble archiving things that were paywalled, even when I was logged in on my phone. In contrast, Readeck will archive what my phone is seeing and store it on my server.

Native.

Samba

Samba provides shared network storage, making it easy to copy files to and from the server, or share important documents with my wife. It’s funny how a file sharing protocol first developed in the 1980s and most associated with Windows remains the best option for cross-platform file sharing on a LAN.

Native.

slskd

IYKYK.

Native.

Snapcast

Snapcast provides whole-house synchronized audio. Think Sonos, but without the expensive vendor lock-in and planned obsolescence. This also deserves its own post. It’s complicated to set up, but it works really well. I eventually plan to purchase some additional devices primarily for use as Snapcast receivers.

Native.

Syncthing

Syncthing is part of a backup strategy for my photos in Immich. I’ve set up a one-way sync (receive only) on my Macbook, so that a copy of all the photos in Immich eventually make their way to my Macbook’s external drive.

Native.

Transmission Daemon

This one is also self-explanatory.

Native.

Uptime Kuma

After a few instances of my wife saying “X isn’t working” and needing to restart a service manually, I realized I needed a way to keep track of what services were running, or not. Uptime Kuma is simple but has a useful set of features. I can ping devices to ensure they’re online, check the status of Podman containers, look for HTTP 2XX response codes from various services, or even parse a JSON payload and extract some details for the health check. If something goes down, I can send a Gotify notification (after a few retries, of course).

Podman.

Vaultwarden

Self-hosted version of Bitwarden. For years, I used KeePass, but never had a good syncing solution, so just avoided logging into things on my phone. Meanwhile, my wife used LastPass, which had various breaches and incidents, besides autofill just not working very well. Migrating her to KeePass was not practical, and I settled on VaultWarden, which is an open-source API-compatible reimplementation of BitWarden that works with the official BitWarden clients. I’m not a huge fan of the BitWarden browser extension, but it’s mostly fine. The Android application is good enough, and syncs seamlessly and automatically when I’m connected to my LAN; otherwise, I can connect via VPN and manually trigger a sync if needed.

I am a little concerned that Bitwarden may eventually become hostile to VaultWarden and break the client compatibility. At this point, the only other major Bitwarden compatible client I’m aware of is Keyguard, which does not have an open source license and uses a freemium model.

Podman.

Vikunja

I’ve been a Trello user for about a decade. But after Trello’s disastrous multi-day outage earlier this year, I decided to find a self-hosted alternative. I ruled out anything that involved spinning up a PostgreSQL or MySQL database for a service that will serve two users. Vikunja uses SQLite by default, though it can be configured to use other database backends. It’s not perfect, and the Android application has some missing features, but it’s good enough for me. Single binary deployment? Yes, please.

Podman.

Yubal

Simple web application to download YouTube Music playlists. I normally use yt-dlp for downloading YouTube videos, or NewPipe for watching on my phone, but Yubal will properly name, organize, and tag music downloaded from YouTube Music.

Podman.

Non-Services

Here are a few things I don’t self-host, tried but decided against, or am unlikely to try.

The *arr Stack

Sonarr, Lidarr, Radarr, etc. Every time I read about setting it up, it just sounds like a resource-intensive mess that’s fundamentally prone to frequent breakage. That’s the opposite of what I’m looking for when choosing self-hosted services.

Collabora Online

While it would be nice to completely part ways with Google, it’s hard to beat Google Docs as a highly convenient and easily accessible way to store and share information. Still, I choose LibreOffice Writer and Calc unless I have a specific reason why the document needs to be in the cloud. Since I already have a shared network drive, it seems pointless to run a service like Collabora Online (a web-based office suite) instead of just using LibreOffice locally.

Firefly III

I tried Firefly III before Actual Budget, thinking I needed built-in support for multiple currencies. It was a complex setup, involving multiple containers, including a container just for importing data. Actual Budget was much simpler to set up and use. For my foreign currency accounts, I have my own simple script to handle exchange rate conversion, so everything in Actual Budget stays in USD.

Owntracks

I like Google Maps Timeline, but after Google limited the location data to the individual device, I hoped to find a self-hosted version. But I could never get the OwnTracks Android application to consistently report my position, no matter how many battery or location settings I tried. Dawarich is another option in this space, but it wants to run “at least” four containers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Sidekiq, web application). For me, that’s not a compelling trade of resources required versus value I’m likely to obtain.

Music Assistant

Music Assistant might work better for you if you don’t already have a music setup you like. In my case, I already had Gonic, Snapcast, and MPD working well. Music Assistant felt like it wanted to “own” everything; for example, it seemed to continually rearrange my Snapcast device groups.

E-mail

Self-hosting e-mail seems like a lot of work for very little benefit. I cannot risk not being able to send or receive e-mails. Eventually I would like to transition away from Gmail to a paid provider.

Conclusion

That’s 17 native services and 11 Podman services, all managed by systemd. htop currently shows about 7.5 GB of memory in use, and CPUs fluctuating between 30% and 40%. It turns out this Mini PC can run a lot! Given how expensive computer hardware has become due to the AI crunch, I hope we’ll continue to see self-hostable projects that prioritize simplicity and efficiency.

[This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

First, they came for the artists,
and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist.
Then, they came for the mathematicians,
and I did not speak out, because I was not a mathematician.
Then, they came for the physicists,
and it was actually really cool and they gave me free tokens and promised to solve my entire field for me and now I can finally devote myself to the important work of publishing papers instead of doing physics

In early October, OpenAI fulfilled every mathematician’s childhood dream.

I am not a mathematician myself (merely a theoretical particle physicist, which some argue barely counts as a scientist either), so I can’t 100% say for certain what inspires someone to pursue mathematics. But, I imagine this dream is common to all academics:

Looking up at the stars in wonderment, or enjoying a complex puzzle game, or being inspired by an encouraging teacher, and dreaming that one day an unfeeling corporate robot[1] will burn a rainforest to compile a list of 700 highly obscure barely-readable facts that *might* be true that nobody can understand as part of a marketing gimmick to raise hype for an IPO[2].

This is probably why most of you reading this got into academia. At least, that’s why I did.

In 1941, Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library containing every possible book that could ever be written. Somewhere in this Library of Babel is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the complete all-orders theory of quantum gravity, and all the papers I will ever write. Of course, there are also incorrect proofs, theories, and misleading Lean certificates, but that is besides the point.

By the research standards of 2026, Borges’s Library of Babel would be the most successful research institution in human history, containing an inconceivably large number of potentially correct mathematical and physical results, blowing OpenAI’s mere 722 write-ups and even the physics community’s recent 2500 write-ups out of the water.

Of course, most recognize that Borges was a visionless fool who failed to recognize the commercial potential of his library, as he never actually built it. He did not have the entrepreneurial STEM-spirit to raise venture capital, launch an IPO, and announce that he had the potential to solve all of mathematics. He was too concerned about the futility of sorting through randomized slop trying to understand what is correct and what isn’t and how to understand it all. But what did Borges know? He was only a writer, and we have already established that artists are obsolete.

Fortunately, OpenAI has brought us one step closer to realizing Borges’s vision. Rather than generating every possible mathematical paper, they’ve found a way to probabilistically generate things that look correct. An important aspect of this increase in efficiency is outsourcing the tedious, unprestigious, and unprofitable work of determining the actual correctness and understanding to the mathematics community (in the past, this was reserved typically for the group writing the paper), while also not wasting any time making the papers human-comprehensible. This is, of course, a tremendous breakthrough. In centuries past, scientists and mathematicians were limited in their ability to solve problems by their ability to understand the solutions. This bottleneck has been removed, and now there is no theoretical limit to the amount of scientific and mathematical factoids we can fail to understand.

From what I know about the academic community (mostly from Twitter and LinkedIn, which I assume are representative), there seems to be near-unanimous agreement that the purpose of math and science research is to gather a large quantity of potentially true factoids in a repository that nobody will actually ever read, in a ritual called “advancing humanity’s[3] knowledge”. That these results are well-written, understandable, pleasant to read or look at, or even completely correct is a secondary concern — in fact, in the pursuit of advancing humanity’s knowledge as quickly as possible, many academics will recoil in anger at the suggestion that it is worth spending any time making results understandable to humans. It is inefficient to explain or check a result when those resources can be spent generating another.

This aligns with my own lived experiences — I didn’t become a theoretical physicist to learn about the universe or better appreciate the beauty of nature myself (that’s philosophy, which I would never be a doctor of). Nor did I spend years learning to write code, make pleasing plots, or craft well-written papers for the simple satisfaction of creating something (that’s art, and we’ve already established that art is obsolete). Rather, I became a physicist to stare at large databases of histograms produced by a Lovecraftian-autocomplete of dubious correctness and say “yeah that’s probably ok I guess” to add to humanity’s knowledge frontier.

I live to serve the knowledge frontier and nothing else.

Math and science are about cold, hard answers, just as art is about producing images, music is about producing sound waves, and literature is about producing strings of text. These things exist to be consumed as content. No rational person, least of all us masters of rationality in STEM, pursues these for the joy of creation, learning, or beauty — all of these are inefficiencies, and we mustn’t be inefficient lest we stifle humanity’s progress. LLMs are not burdened with these inefficiencies, and they will be merely the pursuits of those left behind with nothing more productive to do all day.

Personally, I look forward to the day when ChatGPT can enjoy a sunset or a nice meal on my behalf and free up my time, in the same way I save time on scenic hikes using Uber. And now that AI has solved all our problems, we can devote ourselves to more important work: going into quantitative finance, vibecoding sports-betting apps, consuming AI-generated TikTok shorts, and arguing with political bots on Twitter.

Ultimately, this isn’t just about mathematics or physics — it’s about fundamentally reimagining what it means to be human. By outsourcing the burdens of curiosity, creativity, and understanding, we can finally focus on what matters most: generating value, maximizing productivity, and accelerating progress towards the ultimate goal of science: a complete repo of potentially true facts in a Library of Babel that nobody will bother reading.

And honestly? That’s rare.

By Rikab Gambhir (The @finitephysicist)

Thank you to Terry Tao and Rachel Ward for the opportunity to write a guest blog post! And thank you to Radha Mastandrea, Benoit Assi, Manuel Szewc, Jure Zupan, and Jesse Thaler for their feedback on this essay.

Remember why you chose to go into science and math in the first place!

URL: https://thereallo.dev/blog/someone-on-torrent-sites-kept-fucking-with-my-sonarr-setup, See on Hacker News

I run the usual *arr stack on my NAS. It usually works just fine, until I saw a warning on my dashboard.

The new South Park episode was stuck in the queue with:

WHO is actually falling for this in the big 2026????

Let me very clear about what this is.

Someone took a South Park EP name, put .exe on the end, and uploaded it to public trackers with 2,392 seeders, ???

Who is dropping episodes as an EXE????

And Sonarr grabbed it, because of course it did. Then it sat there trying to import it every 90 fucking seconds:

Not even a folder with a fake .mkv and a "codec installer" next to it like the "good old days".

Just the exe. Are we deadass.

qBittorrent marked it "finished" two seconds after adding it with total_downloaded: 0, so nothing actually landed on disk. No idea why. Don't care. Thanks qBit.

I blocklisted it in Sonarr, which nukes it from qBittorrent and stops it grabbing the same junk skid malware again.

Then I downloaded it again on purpose. Because now I'm pissed and I want to know what's inside.

It's a real PE, x64 GUI. The actual program is 118 KB.

The other 886 MB is random junk glued onto the end. Why? Because a lot of scanners just give up on files that big.

The version info says:

"Freeware Developers." my ass

I chopped the 118 KB off the front and threw it into IDA, because I'm not loading a gigabyte of bullcrap into anything. Then the entire thing is covered in this:

XOR a global. XOR it back. Do nothing. Hundreds of times.

It exists purely to make the decompiler output look like shit, and it does, congrats.

Strip all that out and the logic is like six steps:

  1. Open its own file.
  2. Read the last 64 bytes.
  3. Use those to find and decrypt a payload hidden in the junk.
  4. Map it as a PE in memory by hand.
  5. Point PEB->ImageBaseAddress at it.
  6. Jump in.

Nothing touches disk. Adding all that obfuscation for six steps.

The last 64 bytes of the file are the whole config:

OffsetSizeDescription
0x0032 byteskey, XORed with a 32 byte mask in .data
0x2012 bytesChaCha20 nonce
0x2C4 bytespayload size ^ fnv1a(mask)
0x304 bytes(flags | padding << 8) ^ fnv1a(mask)
0x348 bytespayload size ^ fnv1a(mask)
0x3C4 bytesfnv1a(mask)

It's ChaCha20. They hid the constants by building them out of globals, and they still come out to expand 32-byte k. You can't hide ChaCha20 from someone who's seen ChaCha20 before.

flags = 3 turns on an anti debug check (PEB->BeingDebugged, debug port queries, the usual) and an anti sandbox score. Trip either one and it just quietly exits.

A sandbox sees a normal app open a file and leave.

Cool. Except the key is literally inside the file. (????) You don't even need to run it:

Out pops a second PE. 929 KB, MSVC, C++20, zlib bundled.

All that anti analysis bullshit but a dozen lines of Python can just strip the obf.

Strings are encrypted, imports stripped down to the CRT, everything resolved at runtime.

And then WinMain just dumps every module by name in plain text:

Every other string gets its own function:

Two constants XORed into a key, an IV, ciphertext, length. sub_140080F40 is AES with the S-box hidden behind RC4, because one layer of crypto apparently wasn't edgy enough.

Tried the standard modes on the first one:

AES-128-CTR. Per string key. 672 call sites.

I am not doing that by hand.

So I pulled every call site out of IDA, emulated just the few instructions before each call in Unicorn, grabbed the key, IV and ciphertext out of the registers, and decrypted them in Python. 601 of 672 came out clean.

The rest are buried in bigger functions but I genuinely COULD NOT care less, 601 was plenty.

  • Browsers: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Opera GX, Vivaldi, Firefox. Passwords, cookies, autofill, and it has code for Chrome's new app bound encryption too.
  • Crypto wallets: Exodus, Electrum, Atomic, Guarda, Coinomi, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Wasabi, Sparrow, Monero, Zcash, Armory, plus extension wallets.
  • Password managers: KeePass, KeePassXC, Bitwarden, 1Password, NordPass, RoboForm, Windows Credential Manager.
  • Accounts: Telegram, Discord tokens, Steam, Roblox cookies, Minecraft accounts, Authy.
  • Dev stuff: .ssh, .aws, .azure, gcloud, .kube, .docker.
  • Remote access: AnyDesk, TeamViewer, WinSCP, FileZilla, mRemoteNG, RDCMan.
  • The rest: Outlook, Thunderbird, VPN configs, OBS settings, Sticky Notes, and the documents on your desktop.

It even grabs your Sticky Notes for WHAT????

Everything gets zipped with the bundled zlib and shipped off.

No hardcoded server, instead it decrypts:

A YouTube channel, a GitHub gist, two brackets, and a key that is visibly someone mashing their keyboard.

The YouTube channel is "bubblegym". Created September 14, 2026:

Base64 decode it, XOR it with the keyboard smash, and you get the address:

That exact address is also hardcoded in the binary as a fallback apparently???

I guess the whole point of a dead drop is that you can swap servers without the address being in the malware.

But you put the address in the malware anyway so what's the point for fetching from Gist and YouTube????

Registered September 14. Same day as the "gaming channel". Builds on October 6, torrent up October 8.

If you run Sonarr or Radarr off public indexers, this WILL hit you. Sonarr can't run an exe, so it's not the problem.

The problem is your roommate, your parent, or 3am you double clicking it in the downloads folder. (do NOT execute execute the skid malware)

Five minutes of setup:

  • qBittorrent: add *.exe, *.scr, *.lnk, *.bat, *.cmd to "Excluded file names", tt'll just refuse to download them.
  • Sonarr / Radarr: blocklist with "Remove from client" when you see one of these.
  • Prowlarr: if a tracker keeps serving this crap, demote it or drop it.

And to whoever made this: you probably spent weeks or shit ton of tokens on ChaCha20, AES-CTR, runtime API hashing, anti sandbox scoring, Chrome app bound encryption bypasses, just to make a shitty skid malware.

Get a job.

item.title: Why We're Banning AI (248 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.currentaffairs.org/news/why-were-banning-ai, See on Hacker News

We urgently need to protect human thought and creativity. Our magazine is committing itself to remaining handmade. Ensure every publication you support does the same.

Iam proud to say that as part of our new union contract, Current Affairs recently adopted one of the strictest anti-AI policies in the publishing industry. No text that is AI-generated may be published in our magazine. No AI-generated art may be used as a Current Affairs illustration. When you read Current Affairs, you are going to be reading the thoughts of a human, and seeing the results of human artistry.

We’re adopting this policy because we want to directly challenge the slopification of media. Newsrooms across the country are rushing to embrace AI and replace actual writers, public opinion be damned. The CEO of Business Insider, for instance, has said his publication is “all in on AI” (which is becoming an annoyingly common slogan) and shamelessly publishes AI-written content. At least they’re honest about it. Some publications have deliberately tricked people; Sports Illustrated was caught publishing AI-written pieces by nonexistent journalists. Guest op-eds in all of the major newspapers have been found to be either partly or wholly written by AI. Sometimes publishing this work can happen inadvertently; here at Current Affairs, we have had plenty of freelance submissions that use suspicious numbers of em-dashes and “this is not an X, it’s a Y” sentences. (We can’t promise that nothing will ever slip through the cracks, but we’re vigilant!) Astonishingly, though, some editors have actually defended publishing the pieces even when writers have been caught. The Wall Street Journal published an op-ed from a hedge fund billionaire, Stan Druckenmiller, that turned out to have been AI-generated (probably because billionaires are inarticulate due to a lifetime of never having to craft arguments to persuade the yes-men around them), but the paper defended publishing the piece, since it reflected the billionaire’s genuine opinion.

The trends are dire. But it’s obvious why these publications are rushing to replace writers. They are for-profit corporations, whose ultimate loyalty is to shareholders, not workers. AI is great for them, because it can produce “content” at a fraction of the expense that a writer costs. In fact, on the Milton Friedman theory that the only responsibility a business has is to increase its profits, CEOs are obligated to replace writers with AI if doing so is better for the bottom line. It’s a simple calculation: if producing 100 posts with AI costs almost nothing and takes four minutes, but paying a writer to produce 20 posts costs $5,000, well, why would you pay the writer? The calculation might hold even if the quality drops substantially, errors are introduced, and audience loyalty plummets. Even if you lost 60 percent of your readership, you might still make a lot more per story, because you can pump them out in seconds.

Futurism reports that despite the common narrative that AI has not led to major job loss, creative industries are being “eviscerated” by AI, which is fueling “one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” with more than 200,000 jobs in creative industries being lost in four years. The situation is horrible for artists. Game studios are now designing their worlds and levels using “art assets generated with full AI workflows.” As Brian Merchant reported earlier this year:

Opportunities and pay rates declining as clients and employers embrace generative AI. Artists getting more touch-up jobs and fewer well-paying, sustainable gigs. Pessimism, anger, and even despair, growing common, if not universal, in the field.

This is especially galling given that all of the AI models that are being used to replace artists were trained through the mass theft of those very same artists’ work!

Now here at Current Affairs, we’ve decided to say: fuck that! Over 62 beautiful print issues, we have commissioned hundreds of original, handmade artworks from brilliant artists around the world. We’ve published meticulously researched and edited articles, which often take weeks or months to go from the draft stage to publication. We spend ages working on our page layouts, poring over photographs for the magazine, tweaking sketches, moving sentences around in articles. The labor that goes into this magazine has been extensive from the start, and most of it is hidden from view. We do it because we care about quality. If you pick up a copy of our magazine, you’ll see the result. I think it’s clear when you read it that we actually care about what we’re putting out. It’s not just Content designed to farm clicks.

Current Affairs has always been a bit of an anachronism. We started a print magazine in 2016. Nobody thought this was a good idea. (The editor in chief of Vanity Fair told me to my face that this was a wholly misguided project and certain to fail. I remain grateful to him for giving me the resolve to prove the prediction wrong.) Everyone else was pivoting to video. We pivoted to ink and paper, sent via the U.S. Postal Service. Ten years later, we are still here, while a lot of other places that began with a lot more money have folded (see, e.g., the Messenger, which burned through $50 million in a year and then died). The reason we’ve survived is that there are still many people who don’t like that all media is now just transient images on a social media feed. They experience a thrill when they get a cool thing in the mail that they can unwrap and hold. They know that seeing a beautiful illustration on the printed page is different, and better, from seeing it as a JPEG on your phone.

So we don’t really give a damn what the trends in the industry are. We located ourselves in New Orleans when everyone else is in New York. We defiantly publish on obscure topics that aren’t anywhere in the news cycle. (Have you read Alice Millar-Thompson’s article on eel smuggling?) And we’re going to keep paying human artists to create elaborate, gorgeous works of handmade art that take ages to make.

So our rule is simple: No AI generated articles or illustrations in the magazine! We are not going to feed you slop. And we think you should not give money to any publication that does feed you slop, because they’re both treating their audience with contempt, and avoiding paying workers so that their owners can get richer.

This doesn’t mean nobody doing work here can ever use any of the softwares that are broadly lumped together as AI. Much as we respect the Luddites around here, we’re not against technological innovation. Nothing in our rules prohibits writers from using a new tool to help them research something, or prevents an artist from using a tool to, say, add a texture or change a color, or make some kind of small element. But we need, first, to ensure that technologies are a tool used by workers to help them, rather than a tool used to replace workers. And, second, we need to make sure that readers aren’t being fed things that look like people’s genuine thoughts and creative expression but are in fact the product of disembodied mathematical formulas.

I’ll admit, I used to be excited by generative AI. I made goofy little images in DALL-E. I liked the dumb novelty songs. I thought it could be a cool tool for creative professionals to play around with. I forgot for a moment that we live under capitalism, where every new technology will be used by the ruling class to fuck over workers. As Garrison Lovely writes in his new book Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us—and How to Stop It, the developers of AI don’t see it as an asset for workers, but as a way to replace them. They’re trying to build a device whose success is literally measured by whether it successfully replaces people. It is not being designed to help the average person’s capacity to achieve their goals, but to help automate us all into obsolescence. That’s why it has to be fought aggressively.

We at Current Affairs are not capitalists. There are no profits to be made here. We’re a unionized 501c3 organization, which means that we have no incentive to try to replace our workers with machines. So we’re going to demonstrate that you don’t have to do this, that there’s another way, and that it results in better media that is more pleasurable to read and more informative. It’s not going to be easy, because competitor publications are going to be able to produce immense quantities of writing in the time we are painstakingly correcting and adjusting a single article.

But like John Henry, before we let that steam drill beat us, we will die with our hammer in our hand.

We need your help to keep putting out this handmade magazine. Subscribe or donate today. Your money pays real writers and real artists to make the world’s most beautiful printed publication. If you value authentic human thought and culture, get Current Affairs today.

Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

We believe the future is for everyone, and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.

Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.

It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.

Key Benchmarks

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report.

Optimized for Apple Silicon

Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

Available Now

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

Safety and Preparedness

Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field.

Open weights also carry their own considerations, and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured.

We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card, with a full evaluation report available soon.

License

We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free.

Get Started

You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face.

Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open
